answer.evidence: Under default init (bound 1/sqrt(576)), first-layer weights would fall within about ±69 integer units, so only units whose weights exceed that were clearly shaped by training. Those units all show broad, anatomically sensible patterns. Units 8, 18, 20, 29 (and broadly 1, 2) have large positive weights (up to 85-99) on a central blob, roughly rows 5-21 and cols 5-20. Tracing them through W2 and W3 gives net positive contributions to the logit (approximate integer-product sums: u18 about +32k, u1 about +17.6k, u20 about +10.9k, u8 about +9.6k). Units 17 and 23 have large negative weights in the centre (unit 17 reaches -92 to -97 at rows 8-15) and positive weights around the periphery and border rows/columns (80-89). Their net effect is negative (about -2.4k and -6k), pushing toward benign. Unit 27 is broadly positive over most of the field and contributes about +6k. Many other units look like random init with a slight negative drift. No unit has a compact, high-magnitude, consistently signed patch in a corner or edge, which is what an artificial marker would produce. The closest candidate is a mild positive cluster in unit 9 (rows 14-20, cols 20-22, weights 36-69, all within init range). Weak positive clusters appear in several units at the same spot, but they disagree in output sign; for example, unit 21 is positive there yet feeds strongly toward benign. So it does not form a coherent shortcut pathway, and I treat it as noise.
answer.main_feature: The model mainly measures how much bright, dense tissue fills the central region (nodule size and density). Large, bright central nodules push toward malignant via units 1, 8, 18, 20 and 29, while a dark centre with bright periphery, i.e. small nodules, vessels or chest wall at the edges, pushes toward benign via units 17 and 23.
